subtopics.title: Effects of a and q; find a and q
subtopics.exposition: Functions of the general form y = ax^2 + q are called parabolic functions. In the equation y = ax^2 + q, a and q are constants, and they have different effects on the parabola. The effect of q is called a vertical shift: all points are moved the same distance in the same direction, so the entire graph slides up or down. The standard form of the equation of a parabola is y = ax^2 + q. For q > 0, the graph of f(x) is shifted vertically upwards by q units. For q < 0, the graph of f(x) is shifted vertically downwards by q units. The sign of a determines the shape of the graph. For a > 0, the graph of f(x) is a “smile”. For a > 0, the graph of f(x) is stretched vertically upwards; as a gets larger, the graph gets narrower. For 0 < a < 1, as a gets closer to 0, the graph of f(x) gets wider. For a < 0, the graph of f(x) is a “frown”. For a < 0, the graph of f(x) is stretched vertically downwards; as a gets smaller, the graph gets narrower. For -1 < a < 0, as a gets closer to 0, the graph of f(x) gets wider. To deduce the effect of q, complete a table of values for y = x^2 - 2, y = x^2 - 1, y = x^2, y = x^2 + 1 and y = x^2 + 2 (for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2) and plot the graphs on the same system of axes. To deduce the effect of a, complete a table of values for y = -2x^2, y = -x^2, y = x^2 and y = 2x^2 (for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2) and plot the graphs on the same system of axes.

subtopics.title: Domain, range, turning point
subtopics.exposition: The domain of f(x) = ax^2 + q is {x : x in R} (all real numbers) because there is no value for which f(x) is undefined. If a > 0, the range of f(x) = ax^2 + q is [q; infinity). If a < 0, the range of f(x) = ax^2 + q is (-infinity; q]. The turning point of f(x) = ax^2 + q is determined by examining the range of the function. If a > 0, the graph of f(x) is a “smile” and has a minimum turning point at (0, q). If a < 0, the graph of f(x) is a “frown” and has a maximum turning point at (0, q). The axis of symmetry for functions of the form f(x) = ax^2 + q is the y-axis, which is the line x = 0. For f(x) = x^2, as x increases from -infinity to 0, f(x) decreases. For f(x) = x^2, as x increases from 0 to infinity, f(x) increases. To find the range when a > 0, start from x^2 >= 0 (a perfect square is always positive). Since a > 0, multiplying x^2 >= 0 by a gives ax^2 >= 0. Add q to both sides of ax^2 >= 0 to get ax^2 + q >= q, therefore f(x) >= q. For g(x) = x^2 + 2, the range is found by starting from x^2 >= 0 and adding 2 to both sides, giving x^2 + 2 >= 2, so g(x) >= 2. The range can be read from the graph: for f(x) = x^2, from the graph y >= 0 for all values of x.

subtopics.title: Calculate parabola intercepts
subtopics.exposition: Every point on the y-axis has an x-coordinate of 0. Every point on the x-axis has a y-coordinate of 0. If setting y = 0 leaves an equation with no real solution (for g(x) = x^2 + 2 this gives -2 = x^2), the graph has no x-intercepts. For g(x) = -1/2 x^2 - 3, setting y = 0 leads to -6 = x^2, which has no real solution, therefore there are no x-intercepts. The graph of f(x) = x^2 intercepts the axes at the origin (0, 0). To calculate the y-intercept, let x = 0. The y-intercept of g(x) = x^2 + 2 is found by setting x = 0, which gives g(0) = 0^2 + 2 = 2. To calculate the x-intercepts, let y = 0. An intercept is written as a point with the coordinates separated by a semicolon, for example the y-intercept (0, 2).

subtopics.title: Sketch a parabola
subtopics.exposition: To sketch a graph of the form f(x) = ax^2 + q, determine the sign of a, the y-intercept, the x-intercept(s) and the turning point. To plot a parabola by points, substitute values of x into the equation to complete a table of values. Plot the points from the table of values and join them with a smooth curve. Examine the standard form of the equation: if a > 0, the graph is a “smile” and has a minimum turning point. For the y-intercept, let x = 0; for y = 2x^2 - 4 this gives y = -4, the point (0, -4). For the x-intercepts, let y = 0 and solve; for y = 2x^2 - 4 this gives x^2 = 2, so x = plus or minus the square root of 2. The x-intercepts of y = 2x^2 - 4 are the points (-root 2; 0) and (root 2; 0). Determine the turning point from the standard form of the equation; for y = 2x^2 - 4 the turning point is (0, -4). Plot the intercepts and the turning point, then sketch the graph. Examine the standard form of the equation: if a < 0, the graph is a “frown” and has a maximum turning point. For g(x) = -1/2 x^2 - 3 the turning point is (0, -3), read from the standard form of the equation. For g(x) = -1/2 x^2 - 3, the sketched graph has axis of symmetry the line x = 0.
